reasoning.text: On a still night the coat was laid across the bush, not torn off or blown there. The knife's cork guard lay by the body, so the blade was uncovered at leisure. He took the coat off to have his arms free for some work.
Derbyshire's letters come to Straker's house, his bill was in Straker's pocket, and Mrs. Straker never had the costly dress. The 'friend' is very likely Straker under another name.
A costly milliner's bill for a 'friend' was in Straker's own pocket, and his wife never had such a dress. Straker seems to pay for another woman under another name.

He took an uncorked cataract knife and a candle, laid his coat aside and struck a light in the hollow beside the horse. The sheep by his villa have gone lame. He went out to make a fine cut on the horse.
A cataract knife for fine cuts, a light in the hollow, and lame sheep as if from practice: the harm meant for the horse was a subtle laming of the leg.
The cutting needed a light, free arms and privacy, away from the lad and the loft. That is why the horse was led out to the hollow.
The dog made no noise, so the night visitor was someone it knew. The door was locked at nine and open at seven, and Straker had a key and went out alone at one.

The dog made no noise, so whoever came to the stable that night was someone it knew. The door was locked at nine and open at seven. Straker had a key, went out alone at one, and died beside the horse.
If Straker took the horse out himself, he led it to the hollow where both were found, and he struck a light there.
A trainer who quietly takes out his own favourite at night, with the lad drugged and a surgeon's knife in hand, means it no good.
The silent dog points to Straker as the man who took the horse, and he needed the lad asleep. Only Hunter's portion of the curry from his own house held opium.
If Straker led the horse out alone, past a dog that knew him, Simpson was never in the hollow. The cravat Simpson says he lost must then have been picked up by Straker himself.
